title: Build a paid web app by only reviewing an agent's code
summary: A developer had Claude Code write all application code for 30 days; they say a small paid web app shipped to production, with nine times they had to step in.
agent_role: Claude Code wrote all application code, including sign-in, billing, a dashboard and a public API. The human described tasks, reviewed and approved code, handled settings and secrets, and wrote code by hand in nine logged cases.
outcome: Author reports shipping a working small web app with billing to production, with nine 'breaks' where they had to write code themselves.
what_they_did: A developer set a 30-day rule: Claude Code writes all the app code, and they only describe, review and approve. They built a small paid web app with sign-in, card payments, a dashboard and a public API. If stuck over an hour, they logged a 'break' and coded by hand.
how_it_went: They say setup and routine code went fast and was nearly flawless. Problems came from duplicated helpers, a payment handler that could lose records, fixes that reintroduced bugs, and extra features nobody asked for. The last 10% took three of the four weeks.
worth_knowing: The author's fix: never let the agent that writes code also review it. Use a separate reviewer told to find faults, and a human who approves every merge.
prompt: Help me build [describe your app] using [your preferred tech stack]. I will not edit code myself; you write it and I review. Before each task, show a short plan and list any existing helpers or types you will reuse, so you don't duplicate them. After writing code, switch roles and review your own change as a skeptic: look for failure cases, lost data, and code that works only on the happy path. Keep features minimal unless I ask for more. Never deploy, change payment settings, or merge to the main branch without my explicit approval.

curation.rationale: Honest, detailed field report of building a production app with Claude Code, with nine specific failure points; agent-built web apps are common and the post ends with a product plug.
